articles.author: Oliver Wainwright
articles.title: Take me to the fatberg! The £437m new Museum of London is an astonishing sight
articles.description: After a 10-year transformation, the glorious cathedral-like Smithfields market is now telling the capital’s story. Our architecture critic enters a world of jewels, axes, DJs and dog races – with unposh coffee from Syd’s century-old stall ‘All the grit and the glitters,” trumpets a big illuminated sign on the roof of the old Smithfield general market, beaming out as if advertising a raunchy burlesque show. It is the jazzy tagline of the new-look London Museum, which has gone from being marooned on a roundabout in an armpit of the City to taking over this prime Victorian market complex, following an arduous decade-long transformation. The slogan is fitting for a museum that displays everything from priceless Tudor jewels to a lump of congealed fat and rags dredged from a Whitechapel sewer. Just as the colossal fatberg was scraped from the murky depths, so has the former market hall (and its extensive warren of basement vaults) been meticulously scoured and scrubbed up. London’s centre of butchery for 800 years, which Charles Dickens found “all asmear with filth and fat and blood and foam”, has been lavished with a £437m glow-up, reborn to tell the story of the capital in all its gritty, glittery glory. And the finished result is an astonishing sight. Continue reading...

articles.author: Lucy Mangan
articles.title: Lucy Worsley’s Keys to the Castle review – heavenly TV that instantly brightens up your day
articles.description: The brilliant historian has a gift for cheering everybody up. In this series, she discovers the delights of European castles – and makes you want to spontaneously book a holiday When I think of Lucy Worsley, I am immediately cheered up. Partly it’s the coats. (So neat! So bright! So wonder where she gets them and if I could carry one off!) Partly it’s the hairclips. (How big has she gone this time? Is it going to stay in?) But mostly it is her; her energy, her indefatigability, her determination to impart what she knows in the most accessible way and, above all, her abundant confidence without ego. It’s the latter that allows for that rare thing – other historians to be interviewed and share their knowledge with the lay person at home without the presenter champing at the bit to show that he or she knows this already and that they are just letting them simplify things for the good of the show. This is my personal bugbear, so thank you for letting me exorcise it here, and thank you to Worsley for not adding to my burdens. To feel cheerful as you approach a history lesson is a great boon. To have it be also about one of your favourite subjects is another, and so Lucy Worsley’s Keys to the Castle has me practically insensible with delight before we so much as shift the first tumblers on the lock to the Doge’s Palace in Venice , where the four-part series begins. It then moves on to Versailles and Blenheim before finishing up with – joy of deepest joys, though not perhaps for its poor, lonely conceiver and inhabitant Ludwig II – Neuschwanstein Castle in Bavaria. Continue reading...

articles.author: Adrian Horton
articles.title: Clashing Through the Snow review – Amazon’s Christmas romcom is a bust
articles.description: The Summer I Turned Pretty’s Christopher Briney and 1923’s Michelle Randolph try their best, but this chaotic cross-country journey is not worth taking Credit where credit is due: it takes some nerve for Amazon to open its latest holiday romcom, Clashing Through the Snow, with characters bemoaning the enervated state of the book industry. Publishing isn’t the cultural epicenter it once was, reports boutique press head Jeremy (PJ Byrne) before announcing some impending new year’s layoffs. Alas, things have changed – “if Faulkner were alive today, he’d be making ASMR videos with Mr Beast” (or, perhaps, competing on Prime Video’s Beast Games?) Self-awareness can be key to the ludicrous joys of a Christmas romcom confection, though Clashing Through the Snow, starring 1923’s Michelle Randolph and homegrown Amazon star Christopher Briney (The Summer I Turned Pretty), tests one’s patience for beating you to the branded punchline. Briney’s Ryan, a numbers-driven, macro-counting kind of book editor, pitches a “financial trends with benefits” romance that could be “Rebecca Yarros big”. Soulmates, says Randolph’s rival workhorse editor Hannah, are as mythical as “ethical billionaires and pain-free bikini waxes”. Due to said budget cuts, both have a week to land “a book so big it makes Harry Potter look like a Buzzfeed listicle” for only one to keep their job. What are two LA workaholics going to do on Christmas but take meetings in New York? Continue reading...

articles.author: Editorial
articles.title: The Guardian view on Cop31: a just transition needs more than fine words | Editorial
articles.description: Petrostates blocked ambition while wealthy nations withheld cash support. The climate crisis demands the next UN summit turns promises into action In a negotiation the maxim is usually that no deal is better than a bad deal. But the failure of Cop31 in Turkey to get a climate pact – the first time this has happened in 17 years – should not be an excuse for leaving the planet with the damaging status quo. A hard bargain needs a credible route to agreement: by making commitments, seeking concessions and getting others to reciprocate. This did not happen at the weekend. Responsibility for the breakdown lay principally with petrostates resisting a transition away from fossil fuels and wealthy nations that are unwilling to finance it properly. With the US absent, the EU was foremost among the latter. European governments’ objection to fossil-fuel backsliding by a Saudi-Russian coalition was right, but they were wrong to rule out fresh EU funding for developing countries’ climate action. Despite their reservations, others – notably China and the African group – were prepared to accept a flawed package to keep multilateralism alive. Continue reading...

articles.description: On treacherous political terrain, the government is right to want to proceed with caution and at a pace of its own choosing During the 1980s and 90s, the French president of the European Commission, Jacques Delors, consciously pursued deeper EU integration via a gradualist approach that sought to minimise confrontation. Rather than focusing on ambitious end-goals, risking a showdown with some member states, Delors calculated that taking steps such as the creation of the internal market, in 1993, would eventually generate the momentum to go further. One thing would lead to another, in a logic of deeper union. Mindful of the unique capacity of the Brexit debate to divide and polarise, Andy Burnham appears, for the time being, to be adopting a version of this strategy. On Friday, the prime minister rightly hailed the signing of a reset deal with the EU on food exports, emissions trading and youth mobility as a “good day” for the UK. He then reiterated that further discussion was needed on finding the right long-term relationship with Brussels. Continue reading...

articles.description: Burning the midnight oil playing video games is not ideal preparation for professional sport – but it’s not all bad “They miss games, the cheque’s still clearing. articles.title: Andy Burnham’s EU deal leaves Brexit open to question | Letters
articles.description: Stuart Finegan says the PM deserves credit for his practical steps to rebuild European relations, while Julian Roberts says the point of democracy is surely the right of the people to change their minds. Plus letters from Lindsay Bray , Helen Elliott and Nick Smith Your article ( Burnham seals trade and youth mobility deals in biggest step towards EU since Brexit, 20 November ) marks a welcome moment of political realism after years of denial about the consequences of Brexit. I wholeheartedly agree with Andy Burnham when he said: “This is a good day for Britain and this is a good day for Europe.” For years, the evidence has pointed in the same direction, that the UK economy is worse off as a result of Brexit. Trade barriers have increased, growth has suffered and businesses have been forced to navigate unnecessary bureaucracy. Many of the industries that Brexit supporters claimed would flourish have instead struggled. Fishing, farming, construction and touring musicians have all faced new obstacles, costs and restrictions. Meanwhile, younger generations have seen opportunities to study, work, travel and collaborate across Europe reduced through no fault of their own. The benefits of closer trade links with the UK’s nearest and largest market cannot be overestimated. Yet Nigel Farage and Conservative Brexit supporters have failed to deliver the economic opportunities and global trade advantages they promised. Continue reading...

articles.title: A wake-up call for the UK government on wild birds | Letter
articles.description: Emma Phipps of SongBird Survival writes that the government must act now to save woodland and farmland species from extinction The Office for Environmental Protection’s finding that government departments are breaking the law by failing to protect wild birds should alarm us all ( UK government ‘breaking the law’ by not stopping decline of wild birds, 18 November ). The scale of bird declines in the UK is impossible to ignore, and songbirds are among the worst affected. The Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs’ wild bird indicators show that nearly 70% of farmland songbird species have declined since 1970. Woodland songbirds are faring little better, with more than 30% of species in decline. Unfortunately, none of this comes as a surprise. Decades of monitoring by scientists and dedicated volunteers have shown that our wild birds are in trouble. Yet successive governments have failed to act with the urgency needed to halt these declines. Continue reading...

articles.author: Guardian Staff
articles.title: Sweden’s datacentre politics are more complicated than they appear | Letter
articles.description: There are distinct tensions over who controls, benefits from and gains access to natural and public resources, write James White and Nora Söderberg Steve Rose’s account of Sweden’s datacentre sector ( ‘Datacentres are deeply unpopular. Has Sweden made one we can all love?’, 12 November ) is a welcome reminder that digital infrastructure can be developed in more environmentally responsible ways. However, his suggestion that datacentres have become politically contentious elsewhere, “but here in Sweden, not so much”, is a misrepresentation. Consider the proposed Google datacentre development at Torsboda, near Sundsvall, which requires an enormous allocation of electricity and industrial land. The StoppaGoogle campaign , initiated by the regional political party Norrlandspartiet, has been vocal in challenging what this development will mean for electricity prices, employment and regional development. Controversy over datacentres in Sweden’s north reflect wider debate about resource extraction for the green and technological transitions, and the worry that Sweden is becoming an “electricity colony” of big tech , providing cheap, green energy while the economic benefits are realised elsewhere. At the same time, Sweden-based researchers, such as Julia Velkova , and Jutta Haider and Malte Rödl , have argued that the sustainability of digital infrastructure cannot be reduced to carbon emissions and technological efficiency. Datacentres place high demands on electricity grids, necessitating government investment and compromising access for other industries, communities and public services. While these direct impacts of datacentres are important, so too are the downstream consequences that they overshadow, including how digital services promote climate disinformation and unsustainable mass consumption. Sweden’s renewable energy infrastructure does not make datacentre development environmentally or politically unproblematic, but contributes to distinct tensions over who controls, benefits from and gains access to natural and public resources. Rather than presenting Sweden as an exception to the growing politicisation of datacentres, we should recognise how these conflicts emerge differently in different places, shaped by their histories, infrastructures and political economies. James White and Nora Söderberg Department of Technology and Society, Lund University Continue reading...

articles.author: Berny Sèbe
articles.title: John M MacKenzie obituary
articles.description: Historian who transformed the understanding of empire and its role in shaping modern societies How does ruling the world change the rulers themselves? If such a question has become self-evident today, it was not the case in 1984, when John M MacKenzie, who has died aged 82, published Propaganda and Empire: The Manipulation of British Public Opinion, 1880-1960. Through his analysis of a wide range of cultural artefacts, until then neglected by historians, he articulated some of the key questions that would structure the “imperial turn”. With subsequent publications, and through Studies in Imperialism published by Manchester University Press – a book series that he launched, and edited during three decades, with more than 200 titles now published – he shifted the historical understanding of empire, treating it not as a peripheral aspect of national history, but as a central organising framework for understanding the formation of modern societies, identities, institutions and systems of power. articles.author: John Crace
articles.title: Kemi is beside herself that Burnham is trying to salvage a Brexit deal. Can’t we all stop talking about it? | John Crace
articles.description: Badenoch ends her anti-EU speech by calling herself ‘the leader of common sense’. Really? When you’ve got David Cameron, Theresa May, Boris Johnson and Rishi Sunak saying you’ve got it wrong on Brexit , then the chances are Andy Burnham must be doing something right. These four are the former prime ministers that are largely responsible for the mess the UK is currently in. Lord Big Dave had never really given the possibility of leaving the EU much thought. The Maybot spent three years saying nothing more intelligent than “Brexit means Brexit”. Boris lied through his teeth to get his deal over the line. And as for Rishi? It’s hard to think of anything he achieved. All of which makes life tricky for Kemi Badenoch. Because in an ideal world, Kemi would rather we all forgot about Brexit entirely. Not because it is going so well, but because it it isn’t. She would like you to believe that Brexit was nothing to do with her – even though she was a hardline Brexiter – or the Tories. Rather it was some kind of paranormal event that just happened to the country while the Conservatives were in power. Correlation does not imply causality and all that. In KemiWorld we would pretend that everything is more or less OK and that the noblest course of action is to live with the self-inflicted injury. Continue reading...

articles.title: The best Black Friday beauty deals I’d actually buy, from LED face masks to skincare staples
articles.description: We’ve rounded up the beauty and hair care offers that are actually worth it – all tried, tested and loved by us • The best Black Friday deals • The best Black Friday deals on winter essentials Few of us may be able to justify the cost of a big-ticket TV this Black Friday, but beauty is one area where we can usually afford a treat or two. Thank you, lipstick effect . It can feel like a no-brainer to stock up on our regular favourites and get a few Christmas presents crossed off the list while prices are lower. But deals do something funky to our brains. Retailers know how to lure us in, using big discounts and “selling fast” pop-ups that cause our typically rational brains to short circuit. Add a high-pressure countdown, and before you know it, you’ve been enticed into buying countless products you didn’t set out to buy. Impulse beauty buys are easy to regret later when you snap back into consciousness – not only because of the money you’ve spent, but also because of the waste they create. Continue reading...

articles.title: You Can See Everything tells us nothing about Elizabeth Holmes. I guess that’s what the courts are for | Zoe Williams
articles.description: The Theranos founder talks in frustrating riddles – but was she lying to us, or to herself? Or could she be a cog in a larger, more sinister, lie-machine? I went to see You Can See Everything with a friend who had never heard of Elizabeth Holmes, the disgraced founder of blood testing startup Theranos. She knew that she was a convicted fraudster, because as the film opens, Holmes is 34 days from commencing her prison sentence for defrauding investors. But she was completely open-minded as to whether this was definitely fraud or a miscarriage of justice, whether Holmes was the puppeteer or the puppet (of her previous business and romantic partner, Sunny Balwani, who was also convicted of fraud), and whether Holmes’s central claim, of huge diagnostic capabilities from putting a drop of blood into a tiny box, had any scientific foundation. My friend was probably the co-director Nathan Fielder’s perfect viewer, someone who had no preconceptions about what was true: what would she learn, from three hours with a camera so close to the subject’s face that you could count her eyelashes? “Well … She seems nice?” she said after the film had finished. I veer towards the old-fashioned and deeply held view that the courts, having soberly examined many documents, must have got it right. The whistleblowers and bystanders, giving their testimony not only to lawyers but also to podcasts , which turned into TV documentaries and dramas, as well as investigative print journalism, which begat yet more journalism – that all seemed pretty convincing as well. I definitely did not go into the cinema with my true-crime head on, which is fortunate, because I’m a sucker for a faulty conviction and I’d have probably found her innocent within 15 minutes. Continue reading...

articles.title: Will the Jilly Cooper plagiarism allegations taint our love of Rivals? I doubt it | Nadia Khomami
articles.description: The evidence seems overwhelming, but artists and writers have borrowed from each other for hundreds of years. The line between homage and theft is a thin one “Immature poets imitate; mature poets steal,” the poet TS Eliot wrote a century ago. No work of art, he argued, exists in a vacuum. Great writers draw on what came before them, transforming their influences into something entirely their own. Eliot’s words came to mind when I read the revelations about the queen of the country house bonkbuster Jilly Cooper, who has been accused of “extensive and deliberate” plagiarism in her 1978 book Prudence. At least 35 passages appear to have been lifted from The Serial, a satirical novel by American writer Cyra McFadden, alongside remarkable similarities to sections of Josephine Tey’s 1948 novel The Franchise Affair. McFadden’s daughter is threatening legal action, describing the treatment of her mother’s work as “unconscionable”. articles.description: The manager’s first game in charge was a disaster and he needs to lift the mood within a sunken squad if a relegation battle is to be avoided Sign up for our free newsletter here In as much as any derby can ever be a free hit, there was always a sense that Mauricio Pochettino’s first game as Manchester United manager wouldn’t matter too much; nobody expected them to win away to Liverpool. This was not a game on which anybody was going to judge him, and that feeling only magnified when Leny Yoro was sent off after eight minutes. United’s victory at Anfield last season was their first for a decade; what’s difficult to do with 11 men is only going to get harder playing a man down for 82 minutes. But that does not mean that it did not matter. Although Roy Keane was determined to reject the suggestion, there was perhaps even some credit to be gleaned from having lost only 4-0 . Certainly when they were 2-0 down after 13 minutes, there was reason for United to fear an embarrassment akin to their 7-0 defeat against Liverpool in 2023 . Liverpool had 18 shots in the game three-and-a-half years ago, eight of them on target; on Sunday they had 28, 11 of them on target. When you’ve conceded an xG of 4.38, there’s not much point quibbling over the details; you’ve been hammered. Continue reading...

articles.author: Erica Jeal
articles.title: United Strings of Europe review – they’re the intersection in a Venn diagram of chamber music, string orchestra and jazz
articles.description: Wigmore Hall, London Centred around the world premiere of jazz bassist Misha Mullov-Abbado’s almost-concerto, the tight ensemble took a tour of classical fusion and tango fisticuffs In this eclectic programme of mostly 21st-century music, the United Strings of Europe found the intersection in a Venn diagram of chamber music, string orchestra and jazz. At its centre, receiving its world premiere, was The Travelling Violin by the jazz bassist and composer Misha Mullov-Abbado . In four movements, it’s an almost-concerto on an intimate scale. The solo violin, deftly played here by Tamsin Waley-Cohen, has the narrating role, but the writing for the nine supporting string instruments is so intricately woven that it feels like an ensemble piece. It almost seemed strange for Waley-Cohen to give a solo encore at the end, mesmerising though her playing of Nicola Matteis Jr’s A minor Fantasia was. Mullov-Abbado’s piece has a role for jazz bass, which he played himself, and for percussion, from soft-edged shimmering to driving, grooving drums, played by Fred Thomas; the jazz sensibility of both of these leaches into the rest. Led by the violinist Julian Azkoul, the ensemble was tight, churning over the tricksy rhythmic figures of the faster movements and radiating warmth in the third, which sounded like Cole Porter reflected in a slightly warped mirror. Mullov-Abbado’s violin writing is as gratifying as you’d hope for from the son of Viktoria Mullova , and his jazz-classical fusion hits an unusually effective sweet spot. Continue reading...

articles.author: Xan Brooks
articles.title: Chemicals, Covid and cabbage: why 2026 has been an amazing year for documentaries
articles.description: With Musk, NAZA and You Can See Everything finding large audiences, non-fiction cinema is poised to break through. But there are plenty more gripping stories waiting for their turn in the spotlight There comes a time in the life of every film enthusiast when they must set aside foolish fictions and face up to some hard truths. Specifically, that time arrives each November in the form of the International Documentary Film Festival Amsterdam (IDFA for short), with its tales of crisis and strife, angry resistance and everyday human kindness. The world’s largest documentary festival plays out in the city’s twinkling downtown district, quite near the torture museum, and provides a sharp corrective to the confected dramas and A-list pageantry of Cannes, Toronto and Venice. The forecast is bracing, stormy, and occasionally chilling. Hours of darkness; no stars. We might not wish to live in the world IDFA shows us, but unfortunately we do, and so it pays to stay informed, be engaged. This year’s lineup of 250-plus documentaries steers us around the geopolitical hot spots, from tales of forced displacement in the West Bank to the rolling hell of Gaza; from a jungle-based guerrilla army in Myanmar (in White Tiger Column, the event’s opening night film) through to the traumatised children of the Vietnamese boat people (Carol Nguyen’s superb Still Night, Burning House). Some of these films could have been torn from the headlines. Others, like Raluca Lupascu’s gripping kitchen-sink tragedy A Modern Roma Fairytale, contain stories previously tucked away out of sight, just waiting to be told. Continue reading...

articles.title: Emery insists no change of plan for Aston Villa despite Galatasaray surface
articles.description: ‘Hopefully the pitch will be as best as possible,’ says Villa manager Turkish champions had to move game on Saturday Unai Emery has insisted he will not alter his plans for Aston Villa’s Champions League game at ­Galatasaray on Tuesday night on account of concerns about the state of the pitch. The Turkish champions hastily moved Saturday’s home fixture from Rams Park after starting emergency repairs to the surface this month. The Villa defender Ian Maatsen said he and his teammates were aware the pitch was in a “bad condition”. Villa were informed by Uefa last week that they would be unable to train at the venue the day before the Champions League game in order to give the pitch maximum time to recover after heavy maintenance work. Galatasaray played Saturday’s victory over Samsunspor at Basaksehir Fatih Terim stadium, a significantly smaller ground named after the former Turkey manager, who played for and managed Galatasaray. articles.title: Saariaho’s Adriana Mater transcends horror for hope. Female composers are rejecting opera’s legacy of violence | Annilese Miskimmon
articles.description: The death and pain of female characters has always been a bedrock of opera. Kaija Saariaho and today’s female composers are challenging this narrative, and thereby connecting with today’s world In 1992, the Finnish composer Kaija Saariaho saw a Salzburg festival production of Messiaen’s Saint François d’Assise. A series of meditative theological tableaux in which naturalism and plot is secondary to the revelation of deeper spiritual truths, it is now hailed as a masterpiece although it divided critics on its Paris premiere in 1983. Saariaho, one of the painfully few female composers in opera’s 400-year history, recalled thinking: “If that is an opera, then I can write one”. And she did, to notable international acclaim. Her first opera L’Amour de loin (Love from Afar), a tale of medieval courtly love with a libretto by war correspondent and writer Amin Maalouf was premiered, appropriately, at 2000’s Salzburg festival and came to the UK when English National Opera staged it in 2009 . articles.author: Brian Logan
articles.title: Dylan Moran goes looking for trouble and disappears off the beaten track in this baffling comedy show
articles.description: Royal & Derngate, Northampton The Black Books star gets off to a promising start as he contemplates ‘the burning ball of what you don’t understand’ but his search for levity leads to half-baked ditties Is Dylan Moran joking when he opens his show by telling Northampton’s audience “I didn’t write anything, or prepare”? By the end, you wouldn’t bet on it. Bleary directionlessness may be par for the course for the Irish comic, whose work has always combined poetic-philosophical dazzle with a certain wooziness. But after a promising start tonight, his new touring show, Looking for Trouble, conspicuously loses its way, as Moran frets about forgetting a significant chunk of material, before abandoning his encore and leaving a bewildered audience in his wake. That’s a shame, because there are shards of trademark brilliance in the opening 20 minutes, which see the 55-year-old address himself, albeit obliquely, to the mysteries of being human in 2026, AKA “the burning ball of what you don’t understand” From Trump to AI, Moran surveys it all in wide angle not closeup, as symptoms of our confusion, atavism and fear of expulsion from the tribe. The quality of his thinking in this section, while cheerfully offering himself up as Exhibit A in this prosecution of humanity’s perplexity, is arresting. And there are zingers, too, including a word-picture of the genitals that, once heard, may never be forgotten. Continue reading...

articles.author: Ekin Oklap
articles.title: More sex, different endings: how fan fiction makes our dreams come true
articles.description: From Heated Rivalry to Harry Potter, popular series are inspiring fan fiction read by thousands online. Now the authors of those online works are getting publishing deals of their own Shortly after this year’s London book fair , rumours began to circulate of a seven-figure book deal for the author of the wildly popular work of Harry Potter fan fiction All the Young Dudes. First published between 2017 and 2018 by user MsKingBean89 on the online platform Archive of Our Own, All the Young Dudes is arguably the most-read work of fan fiction of all time. Now its author will write a trilogy under the pen name BN King, with the first novel, Wolfboy, due to be published in autumn 2027. This is by no means the first example of fan fiction crossing over into mainstream publishing: the bestselling debut of 2025, Alchemised, also started off as fan fiction based on the Harry Potter series, with some inspiration from The Handmaid’s Tale too. And nearly 15 years earlier, EL James published Fifty Shades of Grey, which began life as Twilight fan fiction before proceeding, in its new guise, to sell millions of copies worldwide. articles.author: Millie Fender
articles.title: I’ve been covering Black Friday deals for seven years – here are the rules that stop me from overspending
articles.description: Arm yourself with a list, learn how to spot a genuinely good deal and don’t give in to Fomo to shop smarter this season • Expert tips for buying refurbished phones and laptops this Black Friday I’ve been writing about Black Friday deals since 2019, and while you may think spending hours scrolling online retailers’ deals would turn me into a shopping addict, it has (fortunately) done the opposite. Retailers know that, for many of us, this is the time of year we finally buy that hefty investment we’ve been debating, or else blitz through the kids’ letter to Santa. If you play your cards right, it’s an excellent way to save cash. I’d like to think I’ve got my shopping strategy down to a fine art, so here’s how I make Black Friday work for me. Make sure you go in with the right mindset. Relentless discounts and non-stop advertising are designed to make you feel frenzied. When I panic that something will sell out and feel myself rushing to buy it, I find it helpful to close my browser, take a breather, and remember that retailers need my custom more than I need that new coat.
